p: Thursday, December 14. 5:10 AM. The tablet was where he'd left it, face down on the kitchen table beside Ruth's folder, and the coffee maker was doing the thing it did before it worked, which was sigh.

He turned the tablet over. The waiver was still open where he'd left it at midnight. REQUEST FOR WAIVER 62-14, his name typed under an empty line in the board's capitals, and the word nominal in the rationale. Garrett's text sat under it in the notification bar. Sign it in the morning. It was the morning.
He hadn't recorded a log to Ada since Tuesday. Grace's chair was pushed in at the end of the table the way it always was, and he didn't look at it, which was its own way of looking at it.

He shaved. He put on the gray suit he'd bought for Bea's going away, which nobody had held, so it had never been worn. He put a pen in the inside pocket of the jacket, the left one, where the jet's forms had gone in Arizona. Then he stood in the hall for a while with his hand flat on the pocket, the way you'd check for a wallet.

On the counter by the door the envelope to Ruth was under his keys, where it had been since February. The photocopy was still in it, with STILL ASKING beside the third row in Nell's blue ink, and it was still unsealed. He picked up the keys. He left the envelope.

At 5:50 he backed out of the driveway into a cold that had come down off the mountains in the night. Twenty miles east, over the high bay doors, the clock said 66. He was driving the other way. Downtown there was a federal building with a fourth floor he'd been in twice, and the coffee there was bad both times.
Ruth's Console Log, page thirteen: The door in it.

Ruth's console log. Petrel. After. L Plus 282 Days. March 20 2036. oh six hundred, kitchen. coffee. legal pad. green pen. house quiet. oh six ten, draft 9. flight rule 2.36. oh six fifteen, line 1. no crit 1 anomaly closes unexplained without 3 independent repro attempts and the fd's signature. oh six forty, why 3. two is what we had time for. oh seven hundred, read it to the window. who finds the way around it. oh seven oh five, downgrade it first. then it isn't crit 1. that's the way. oh seven ten, line 2. no crit 1 is downgraded without the same 3 attempts and the same signature. ten hundred, agency, 7TH floor. counsel read it. the administrator's deputy read it. ten forty, line 2 struck. too broad. a rule nobody can meet isn't a rule. ten forty one, told them somebody will meet it by downgrading. deputy said that's what engineering judgment is for. ten forty five, signed line 1. let line 2 go. fourteen hundred, rule 2.36 in the book. my name on it. seventeen thirty, L plus 282. a rule with a door in it. I know where the door is.

I wrote nine drafts of that rule at the table you've sat at, and the ninth is in the book you fly under. You'll have seen the door already. You found a report in your first month that walked through it: a criticality 1 anomaly downgraded to criticality 2 eleven days before a review, so that my rule showed NOT APPLICABLE beside it, in my own agency's capitals.

I knew at seven in the morning how it would be done. I wrote the line that would have stopped it. By eleven it was gone, and I signed what was left, because a rule with a door in it seemed better than no rule, and because I was tired, and because the people who struck it were people I'd have to work with for twenty more years. Each of those reasons was true. Put together they come to the ten forty five line.

This chapter is about the moment somebody hands you a paper and a pen. A waiver, a status report, a rationale with one word in it you don't believe. It's about who's allowed to say yes to a risk, how you say no in a way that does some good, what the Code asks of you when the room would like you to sign, and how to stand in a public room and tell the truth to people who all want different things from it. And it's about the culture that makes a door in a rule feel like a reasonable place to walk.

How the exam asks it. When you're asked to sign or approve something you believe is inaccurate or unsafe, the PMI answer is to decline, state your reasons, present the facts and options to the right authority, and let governance decide. Signing "because they'll decide anyway" is the distractor.

The exam outline puts ethics inside governance, which is where it belongs. B1 asks you to describe and establish the structure, rules, procedures, reporting, ethics, and policies of the project, using the organization's process assets, and to outline the escalation paths and thresholds. Read that as one question asked many ways. For every decision that could matter, who decides, who has to be asked first, and what happens when they disagree.

Risk is where the question bites hardest. The PMBOK Guide's risk domain, section 2.7, gives you two words worth learning exactly. Risk appetite is how much uncertainty an organization or a person is willing to accept for a reward. Risk threshold is the measurable line that expresses it, the variation around an objective that's acceptable. An appetite is a feeling; a threshold is a number somebody wrote down before the data came in. You want the number.

Then there's whose decision a risk is. The Guide's risk response strategies, in section 5, say that a threat outside the project's scope, or a response beyond the project manager's authority, gets escalated to the level that matches the objectives it would affect, and that the ownership of an escalated threat has to be accepted by the party it goes to. Accepted. Somebody has to take it, by name. A risk you've sent upstairs that nobody took is a risk nobody owns.

On a program that carries people there's one more rule, and the better space programs write it down in so many words. Residual risk to the people who'll fly is accepted by the authority set up for it, in writing, and the people who'll bear the risk consent to it, formally, through their own chain. The contractor doesn't accept it for them, and the program manager never accepts it alone: the safety and technical authorities have to concur. On Halcyon the board's rules go further and keep it with the board. The person whose life is in the risk gets asked.

How the exam asks it. A risk beyond the project manager's authority is escalated to the level that matches the objective it threatens, and that party must accept ownership. Accepting it yourself, or letting the contractor accept it, is wrong.

Programs that live under requirements have two words for permission to miss one, and the difference is time. A deviation is permission, given in advance, not to meet a requirement before it's been put under configuration control. A waiver is permission not to meet a requirement that's already baselined, usually because something was built, tested, or found that doesn't conform. A deviation is a decision about a plan. A waiver is a decision about a thing that exists and doesn't do what it was supposed to.

Either way the requirement stays. A waiver doesn't change the rule; it records that this case won't meet it, why, and who agreed. It's a risk acceptance wearing a different hat. If you remember one thing about them, remember that. When someone asks for a waiver, they're asking somebody to accept a residual risk, and every question from the last section applies. Who has the authority? Has the person exposed to it agreed? What does the rationale actually say?

And look hard at how a waiver gets around the thing it waives. My rule was gotten around by a downgrade, which made the waiver unnecessary, which is the cleverest kind. The other way is the rationale. A waiver that says the data are nominal, when the data show a pattern nobody understands, is asking the signer to agree to a description, not to a risk. Read the rationale as if your name were under it. On some days it will be.

How the exam asks it. A waiver doesn't remove a requirement or a risk. It documents an accepted exception, by the right authority, with rationale. Treat a waiver request as a risk acceptance decision.
When somebody hands you a pen.

The Code has four values, responsibility, respect, fairness, and honesty, and under each it has two kinds of standard. Section 1.5 explains the difference. Aspirational standards are what we strive for, and they're hard to measure. Mandatory standards are firm requirements, and breaking them can bring you in front of PMI's Ethics Review Committee. One act can break both. The exam likes to ask which is which. The job mostly asks whether you'll do either.

Responsibility, 2.1, is the duty to own the decisions we make or fail to make, and the actions we take or fail to take. The aspirational 2.2.1 says we decide in the best interests of society, public health and safety, and the environment. The mandatory side starts with 2.3.1, uphold the policies, rules, and regulations that govern our work, and 2.3.2, report unethical or illegal conduct to appropriate management and, if necessary, to those affected by it.

Honesty's mandatory standard is the one you'll meet most often with a pen in your hand. 5.3.1: we don't make misleading or false statements, state half truths, give information out of context, or withhold information that would make what we say misleading or incomplete. A signature under a rationale is a statement. If you sign a document that describes the data in a way you know misleads, you've made the statement, whoever typed it.

Respect has a mandatory line people forget is there. 3.3.2: we don't use the power of our expertise or position to influence the decisions or actions of others to benefit ourselves at their expense. A chief executive who asks a project manager to sign so that an old phone call stays private is doing exactly that, even when he's frightened, even when he's sorry. And fairness, 4.2.1, asks for transparency in how we make decisions, which is the thing a signature on a waiver is supposed to show.

So what do you do? Not only refuse. Refusing and going quiet leaves the misleading paper as the only written thing in the room. Decline, in writing. Say why, specifically. Put the data and the options in front of the people with the authority to decide, and say what you recommend. Then let them decide, and live with it, and write down your dissent if you have one. That's the whole method. It's slower than signing, and it costs more in the hall.

How the exam asks it. For "sign it or else" questions: don't sign what you believe is inaccurate, don't stay silent either. Document your position, give the facts and options to the decision authority, and escalate through governance.

Some words round numbers without touching them. Nominal is one. On track is another. Green. Within limits. Performing as expected. Each of them can be true in every letter and still leave the reader believing something the data don't say.

The PMBOK Guide is plain about this in a place you might not look, the Resources domain, where it describes how a project manager models integrity for a team. Honesty, it says, looks like sharing risks, communicating your assumptions and the basis of your estimates, delivering bad news early, and making sure status reports give an accurate depiction of the project's progress. The Standard's principle, Be an Accountable Leader, asks for integrity, honesty, and fairness, especially in tough situations. That's the standard for a status line.

The exam outline's R9, evaluate project status, asks you to develop the metrics, measure and analyze them, and communicate status, and to make sure the artifacts are created, reviewed, and kept up to date. In practice that means a status that shows the measurement, the limit, the trend, and what nobody knows yet. Every close was inside its limit is a measurement. Every third close after a soak rippled, and we don't know why, is the trend and the unknown. Leave either one out and the reader has a different valve than you do.

There's an opposite failure, and good people fall into it when they've been burned. They lead with the worst case so the decision goes the safe way. That's steering too. Give the people deciding the same picture you have, evenly, with your recommendation said as a recommendation, and trust them with it.
How the exam asks it. When results are inside limits but show an unexplained pattern, report both: the measurements against the limits and the open question. "All results nominal" is the half truth.

Every serious program has people who'll disagree with a decision, and the healthy ones give them a way to do it that isn't a hallway. The better space programs teach three choices to every member of a team. Agree. Disagree, and fully support the decision anyway. Or disagree, and raise a formal dissent.

A formal dissent is written down, and it goes up, at least two levels above the decision it disagrees with. When there's time, the people who disagree write it together: the facts they agree on, each position with its rationale and its impact, and each side's recommendation, approved by both. That last part matters more than it sounds. When two people have to agree on the facts before they argue, half the argument usually goes away, and the half that's left is the real one.

Boards do the same thing in their minutes. A vote that isn't unanimous carries the dissent beside it, attached, with the member's reasons, so the next person who reads the decision reads the disagreement too. A dissent in the record is information the organization gets to keep.

None of this works if people pay for it. The Code's 2.3.5 says we don't retaliate against people for raising good faith ethical concerns, and that retaliation is subject to discipline, and its aspirational 5.2.5 asks us to make an environment where others feel safe to tell the truth. Write both into the process: a dissent can't cost anybody a job, a program, or a seat in the next meeting. Then check, a month later, that it didn't.

How the exam asks it. When a team member disagrees with a governance decision, the PMI answer is to document the dissent with the facts and rationale and route it through the escalation path, protected from retaliation.

A public hearing is a stakeholder map with chairs in it. The sponsor in the front row. The contractor at its own table. The families with their binder. The press with a camera at the back. The crew, who'll ride whatever is decided. Each of them came for a different reason, and each will hear a different thing in the same sentence. The outline's P4 asks you to identify and analyze them, tailor communication to their needs, and build trust. P6 asks you to know what your customers expect and keep monitoring it and answering it.

Two habits help in a room like that. First, say the same facts to everyone. The Code's fairness side, 4.2.3, asks for equal access to information for the people authorized to have it. If the board has every trace, the crew should, before the board does if you can manage it. The people who carry the risk shouldn't learn about it from a docket notice at six in the morning.

Second, don't play to the gallery. A public room tempts you to say what will land well on the feed. Say what's known, what isn't, and when the decision comes, and say it the same way to the camera as you'd say it to the crew. People can live with uncertainty when it's told to them straight. What they can't forgive is finding out later that you knew.

And disclose your own interests before anybody else does. Code 4.3.1 and 4.3.2 ask you to disclose real or potential conflicts, and to stay out of the decisions they could bend until there's a mitigation and consent. A disclosure in a public room lets the room trust the rest of what you say.

How the exam asks it. In public or high-pressure settings, the best answer gives every stakeholder the same accurate information, discloses conflicts, and explains what's known, unknown, and when the decision will come.

The outline's B7 asks you to assess organizational culture and to evaluate how a change in the organization affects the project. When a failure turns out to be organizational, and most of them do, culture is where you look, and it's never where the slide deck says it is.

Culture is what happens at nine forty at night when somebody important calls somebody tired. It's what gets rewarded and what quietly gets punished. It's whether the person who says no finds out from the work order. You don't learn it from the values on the wall. You learn it by asking the people who live in it a plain question and listening long enough: when something here doesn't look right, what happens next?

Then change something real, with them. New rules handed down by memo, the week after a hearing, usually get a joke for a nickname. Rules written by the people they're meant to protect get used. And the change has to start at the top with somebody saying, in front of everyone, what part was theirs. People believe a culture has changed when a leader pays for the old one in public. They don't believe it any sooner.

How the exam asks it. Before changing processes after an ethical failure, assess the culture with the people affected, and have leaders model the change. A memo or a hunt for whoever spoke up are distractors.
I've told you about the ten forty five line now. I told it last week, in a room full of strangers. It didn't make anything right. It did put the door on the record, where somebody else could see it.

You'll write rules of your own someday, on a program of your own, and somebody will strike the best line in them for a reason that sounds sensible on a Tuesday. Fight for it. If you lose, write down what was struck and why, and put your name beside it, so the next person knows where the door is. Then watch it. Doors don't stay shut because you know about them. They stay shut because somebody keeps standing in front of them.
How the exam asks it. Ethics questions usually have one answer that's slower, more uncomfortable, and goes through the proper authority. That's the one.
6:05 AM. I-70 westbound, past the old stockyards, with the city lit up ahead of him and the mountains still black behind it. The dash said IMOGEN HALE, and he answered it.

I read it at midnight. So did eleven partner liaisons, because the docket goes to them automatically, which I've asked to have changed four times. She sounded like she'd been up since. I want you to ask Esther Quayle for a continuance on item one. January 4. The partners' finance committee takes up the sixteen million on Monday. If a waiver fight runs on Greaves's feed all weekend, we lose it, and if we lose it we're short in February. And nobody makes a good decision about a valve the week before Christmas.

The board's rules let a party ask for a continuance before a session opened. The chair usually gave one to a program. She'd almost never give one to a sponsor, and Hale knew it, which was why she was calling him.

Quinn's email had come in at 11:58 PM, after the docket, with no greeting. Aldergrove's valve finishes acceptance Wed Dec 20. Coquina closes the crew launch manifest Fri Dec 22 at 5 PM. If the board decides after the 22nd, the valve doesn't fly on the 9th, and the spacewalk is gone without anybody choosing it.
Hale went on before he could answer. I said February 2063 on camera in 2058. I've said it to eleven governments every year since. I'm not asking you to sign anything. I'm asking for three weeks.
The light at the Brighton Boulevard exit went red. He had a little under three hours.
Hale asks Sam to get the board to grant a three week continuance. How should he respond?
A. Ask the chair for the three week continuance before nine, as the sponsor has requested.
B. Tell Hale the board's calendar isn't hers to set, and end the call to get ready for nine.
C. Pass Hale's request to the chair as hers, without a view of his own, and let the chair weigh it.
D. Tell Hale what a continuance would decide by itself, and ask her to make her case to the board.

He pulls into a gas station on Brighton Boulevard and talks to her for twenty minutes with the engine running. The manifest date. What a continuance would decide by itself. What he'll say at nine, and what he won't. She doesn't like any of it, and she says so. At 8:31 the clerk adds a line to the docket: THE DIRECTOR OF THE ARA WILL ADDRESS THE BOARD ON PARTNER FUNDING. If I'm going to lose sixteen million, she tells him in the hall, I'd like to do it myself, out loud.

That's a go. Engage the stakeholder: hear the concern under the request, show her the fact that changes it, tell her plainly what you'll do, and give her a legitimate way to be heard by the people who decide. Agreeing with her would have been easier, and it would have let the calendar pick the valve.

7:20 AM. The fourth floor of the federal building had a witness room off the hearing room, with a table and six chairs and a box of tissues somebody had put out for other kinds of hearings. Garrett was in it when Sam came past with his coffee. He said, Close the door, in a voice Sam had never heard him use, which was a quiet one.
He wasn't smiling. Sam had read that smile like a gauge for two years, and the gauge was off.

Thursday, September 18, 2059. I had dinner in Cherry Creek with the two biggest names on our cap table, and I told them the review on the thirtieth would be clean. Then I called Hana at home. Nine forty. I told her I needed a recommendation in the morning that I could take into that room, and that it had to close. I told her the stand was booked that week for the qualification firing. It was. I'd booked it that afternoon, over Wendell's slot.

Garrett turned his coffee cup a quarter turn on the table. She asked about the third attempt. I said after the review. She said okay. That's the whole call. Four minutes. Bea timed the meeting the next morning at twenty two. Nobody timed mine.

He looked at the box of tissues as if it had said something. She's carried it for three years like it was hers. Some of it was. Most of it was mine. Nobody did it alone. I did more of it than anybody.
You've known since your first month that the closure was wrong. So have I.

So here's what I need, and I know how it sounds. Sign the waiver. The workaround works. Wendell's runs say so. If you sign, this morning is about engineering. If you don't, Esther Quayle asks you why, and the answer is 2059, and 2059 is me, on Greaves's feed, with the partners voting on Monday.
Out in the hall the clerk was unlocking the hearing room. Somebody laughed at the coffee urn, the way people laugh at a coffee urn at seven in the morning.
Garrett has told Sam his part in 2059 and asked him to sign the waiver. How should Sam answer him?
A. Keep Garrett's account between the two of them until the waiver question is settled.
B. Tell Garrett his 2059 call goes into AR 2207's record this morning, in his words if he wants.
C. Offer to sign the waiver if Garrett puts the 2059 call in AR 2207's record himself today.
D. Write down what Garrett said, word for word, and send it to the clerk before nine without telling him.

Thank you for telling me. I mean that. Then the rest, in order. It goes into AR 2207's closure history, where Hana's account and Bea's went, and the board hears it this morning. In his own words, if he wants it that way, and Sam will sit next to him while he says it. If he doesn't, Sam will tell the board that an account exists and who has it, and nothing more. And the waiver is a different question with its own answer, which Sam will give at eight thirty. Garrett looks at him for a long time. Then he takes a legal pad out of his counsel's bag and writes for twenty minutes, standing up, and gives it to the clerk himself at 8:50. ACCOUNT OF G. LYLE FOR THE CLOSURE HISTORY OF AR 2207. Two pages. The call is on the first one, with the time.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Respect the person, then report through governance. A leader's part in a safety closure that went around a flight rule is a compliance matter the record has to hold (Code 2.3.1, 2.3.2). Let him own it in his own words, and don't let it be traded for anything.

8:15 AM. The clerk had set out the morning's papers on a table outside the hearing room in docket order, and the waiver was third, under the agenda and the program's data package. Somebody at Tallgrass had stuck a yellow tab on the signature line.

The board's rules were in a binder beside it. Rule 9: a request for waiver of a criticality 1 requirement comes to the board signed by the program manager of record, or with the program manager's written statement of nonconcurrence, and the board hears it either way. Rule 11: residual risk to crew is accepted by the board, in writing, or it isn't accepted.
Quinn had texted at 7:58. Package is right. I checked it again at 11. Every run is in it. Nothing in it says nominal. Hana had texted at 8:02, one line. Whatever you do, I'll stand behind the data.

Wendell came off the elevator at 8:10 with Arlo a step behind him. Wendell was in a tie he said he'd last worn in 2036 and a jacket that wasn't canvas, and page twelve was folded in his shirt pocket, behind the doctor's note, where it always was now. Arlo had borrowed a tie from his brother in Limon. It was too long, and he kept tucking the end into his belt.

Garrett's counsel came out long enough to put a pen on the table beside the waiver, a good one, and went back into the witness room. Garrett was still in there with the legal pad. Through the glass in the door Sam could see him writing, standing up, and crossing something out, and writing it again.

The word was still there. GROUND RUNS WITH THE WORKAROUND NOMINAL. Every run had been inside its limits. The third close after every soak had rippled, 2 milliseconds after lift, and nobody knew why. The drawing said revision D on MOIV-1's position sensor harness, and the valve on orbit had revision C, and nobody knew why that was either.
Garrett's counsel has left a pen beside the waiver. What should Sam do with the signature line?
A. Decline to sign, and file a short written statement of nonconcurrence with the clerk.
B. Leave the signature line blank and let the board take up the request as Tallgrass filed it.
C. Sign it, and clip on a handwritten note that lists every open item and his doubts.
D. Sign the waiver and let the board weigh the request on the data it hears at ten.

He writes it at the clerk's table on the back of the agenda, types it on his phone, and sends it to the clerk at 8:37. STATEMENT OF NONCONCURRENCE, S. OKAFOR, PROGRAM MANAGER. Five sentences. He doesn't sign Request for Waiver 62-14. The ground runs met their limits, and the third close after every soak rippled 2 milliseconds after lift, cause unknown; the word nominal leaves that out. Revision C against D is unexplained. The program will present both options with their risks and dates and recommend from the data. Acceptance of residual risk to the crew belongs to the board under its Rule 11, with the crew's consent, and isn't the program's to give. He puts the good pen back where counsel left it.

Exactly right. Don't sign what you don't believe, and don't only refuse. Put your position, the data, and the options in writing through governance, and leave risk acceptance with the authority that has it. That's responsibility and honesty together (Code 2.2.1, 5.3.1).
8:40 AM. Commander Haddad came up the stairs instead of taking the elevator, two at a time, in a flight jacket over a sweater, with her phone in her hand and the docket on its screen.

Haddad had been home in Aurora since Monday, her last two weeks before quarantine. She'd read it at six, she said, in her kitchen, with her youngest eating cereal beside her. Nobody had sent it to her. The partners' liaisons got the docket automatically. The crew didn't.

Root cause to continue during cruise. She read it off the screen. During cruise is us. That's two hundred days of four people and a valve nobody understands, on the far side of a burn we've already done. Is this your waiver, Sam?

At the window at the end of the hall Ilse Brandvold was looking down at the street with her hands in her jacket pockets. Mateo Echeverría and Dr. Rao were on a video call on Brandvold's tablet, from Houston, waiting to hear what Haddad said.
His statement of nonconcurrence had gone to the clerk three minutes ago. The crew hadn't seen that either.
The board's rules gave the crew a seat in the room. They didn't give the crew a place on the docket unless somebody asked for one.
Haddad read the docket at six and asks whether this is Sam's waiver. How should he answer her?
A. Point her to the board's clerk to ask for the crew's own place on this morning's docket.
B. Go through the whole package with the crew now, and ask the chair to hear them on the record.
C. Tell her the waiver is between the program and the board, and brief the crew fully once it rules.
D. Give her a short summary now and the full data after the ruling, to spare the crew's last week.

He sits down with all four of them on the bench by the window, two in person and two on the tablet, and goes through the package page by page with Quinn: every run, the ripples, the 40 milliseconds on orbit, the harness revision, the things nobody knows. He tells Haddad where he stands on the waiver and why. Then he asks the clerk for the crew to be heard. The clerk adds it at 8:58: ITEM 1. THE COMMANDER OF HALCYON WILL ADDRESS THE BOARD FOR THE CREW. Haddad reads it on her phone and puts the phone away. Okay. Now we're in it.

That's a go. The crew carry the risk, so they're the first stakeholders to know it fully. Give them the same data the decision makers have, tell them your position, and make sure their voice reaches the people deciding. The people who bear a risk should consent to it on the record.

9:00 AM. The hearing room had the same terrazzo in the hall and the same coffee in the urn, and a bench of pale wood across the front with six chairs behind it and a seal on the wall that the ARA had paid for and the building's lease said it couldn't take down.

Greaves's crew had a camera on a tripod at the back. Frances Odum was in the third row with the Families of Ares binder on her knees. Hale was in the front row, still in her coat. Nell Garrity sat on the aisle with her father's badge on its frayed lanyard, and nodded to Sam when he came in. Wendell and Arlo were in the second row, beside the crew. Lorna Whitcombe was in the fourth, with a pad on her knee.

Ruth was second from the left on the bench, in the gray cardigan, with the green pen clipped in its pocket and a typed page face down in front of her. She didn't look at the program's table. She didn't look anywhere in particular, which on Ruth was a decision.

The chair was a woman of sixty eight named Esther Quayle, who'd spent thirty years on a range safety console and had the voice for it. She called item one at 9:02. Before the clerk could read it, Ruth said, Madam Chair. Before this item, a disclosure.

I was the flight director of the Petrel. On May 28, 2035, I signed waiver 35-114, which let an isolation valve of this family fly with an unexplained anomaly, closed at criticality 2. The test conductor of record on this item sat my propulsion console then. And since January of last year I've sent the program manager pages of my own console log from the Petrel, one at a time. They're about a ship that's gone, and they say nothing about this board's business. He came to my kitchen once, in January of last year, to ask how the board wanted to be told things. I told him. We haven't discussed this board's business since. You should still know about all of it. I'll step down from this item if the board thinks I should, and any party may ask it to.
The room went quiet the way rooms do when a camera is on and everybody remembers it. At the back, Greaves didn't move.

The chair let it sit. Under our rule 4, a member with a disclosed interest sits unless the board, after hearing the parties, decides otherwise, and the disclosure goes in the minutes. Tallgrass? Garrett's counsel looked at Garrett. Garrett said, No objection. The program. Mr. Okafor?
The chair asks whether the program objects to Member Calder sitting. How should Sam answer?
A. Ask that her pages to him stay out of the minutes, and raise no objection otherwise.
B. Consent to her sitting, and add a disclosure of his own to the same minutes.
C. Tell the chair the program has no objection to Member Calder sitting on this item.
D. Ask that Member Calder step aside from this item, given her long history with the valve.

The program consents, ma'am. And a disclosure of my own, for the same minutes. I've received those pages, twelve of them, since January of last year. And my daughter, Ada Okafor, is on Ares Station. Anything on this item that touches crew safety or the colony's margin is the board's to decide, not mine. The clerk writes. The chair asks the other members one at a time, and all four consent, and she reads the mitigation into the record: any member may ask that Member Calder's vote on the item be explained in writing. Ruth doesn't look at him. She turns her typed page over.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Support the board's process for a disclosed conflict (Code 4.3.1 and 4.3.2: disclosure, a mitigation, consent), and match her honesty with your own. Disclosing the relationship from your side keeps the record complete and the board's independence visible.

9:14 AM. The chair said the board would hear the member's statement before the item, at the member's request, and that it would be part of the record. Ruth turned the typed page over, put her reading glasses on, and then didn't read from it.

I've never said this in public. I said it to an investigation board in 2036, in a room like this one, and they wrote it down, and it went into a report people quote my rule from and don't read. So I'll say it once in a room where it might be some use.

On October 18, 2034, an isolation valve on the Petrel's departure stage disagreed with itself for forty milliseconds on the third close of five. We ran it twice more that morning. Both clean. My propulsion console told me nobody could tell anything from two retests the same morning, and asked for the spare valve on the stand for five hundred cold cycles. I wrote down five hundred. I didn't ask him why. I found out why fifteen months later, from the investigation board's clerk. The retests had run warm.

Ruth said it to the room, not to the bench. In December I rounded a cost index for the Administrator. In February the same man asked me if the crew knew about cycle three, and I told him the crew had enough to think about. In April the valve's maker asked me for three weeks and a change order to run his spare cold, and asked if I'd looked at his row three. I told him I'd looked at the schedule. That was true.

On May 28, 2035, fifteen days before the window, I signed waiver 35-114. Nobody in the room told me to. Nobody had to. That afternoon the commander, Lise Arnaud, came to my console in her flight suit and asked me if I was sure. I said yes. I said it the way you say it to somebody you want to stop worrying.

She stopped and drank some water, and the clerk's pen stopped with her. On June 12, on the poll, my propulsion console answered first, the way he always did. He said go. He took a second before he said it, and I heard the second, and I said the flight director is go, and my voice sounded fine. At cutoff the valve didn't close. A minute later we had nothing. We never found out why it didn't close. The valve went with the ship, and Lise Arnaud and Kenji Mori and Roz Tate went with it.

In March of 2036 I wrote the rule this board works under. Three independent attempts to reproduce, and the flight director's signature, before a criticality 1 anomaly closes unexplained. I wrote a second line, that a criticality 1 couldn't be downgraded without the same three attempts and the same signature. The agency's lawyers struck it as too broad. I let them. I knew exactly how somebody would get around my rule, and I signed it with the door in it.

Ruth looked down at the typed page for the first time, and then didn't use it. The families were never told about the valve. Roz Tate's mother asked on television why not, and nobody answered her, because counsel had told us not to, and I was one of the people who didn't. My husband had bought me a telescope the Christmas before, so I could watch the ship go. It's in my garage. I haven't opened the case.

The man who took that second on the poll is in the second row of this room. I asked him once, in a hall, in 2036. He told me to ask him again sometime. I never have, and I'm not going to ask him here. This isn't his hearing, and it isn't mine. I've told you all this so you'll know what my vote on this item is made of. Now I'm going to try to cast it on the data, like the rest of you.

She took her glasses off. Nobody said anything. In the second row Wendell had his hand flat on his shirt pocket, over page twelve, and he kept it there. At the back the camera's red light was on, and fifteen minutes later, give or take, so was every screen in the galley on Ares Station.
10:50 AM. After a recess nobody had asked for and everybody needed, the chair called the program. Mr. Okafor. The program's data, then Tallgrass on its request. Take the time you need.

Quinn had the package on the screen. Forty commanded closes on the ground in the workaround campaign since November 9, thirty nine completed, every one inside its limit. The third close after every soak, eight of eight, with a ripple 2 milliseconds after lift. Hot fire 2's cycle three at the Cape in September, 7 milliseconds, inside the 10 millisecond limit. The 40 millisecond disagreement on orbit in October. The lot valve's runs, which had taught everybody a great deal about what the cause wasn't. Revision C against D, unexplained. The blind reads, and the one trace that had been missed.
Down at the end of the bench Member Ferris had the ripple table open. He'd boxed the third row in pencil, twice.
Quinn has the whole package on the screen. How should Sam present the runs to the board?
A. Walk the board through every run against its limit, with the unknowns and both options.
B. Summarize the package as filed, and let Hana and Wendell take the members' questions on the ripples.
C. Present the runs the way the waiver does: every close inside its limits, root cause work ongoing.
D. Open with the Petrel and the worst case on orbit, and put the traces up after that.

He takes forty minutes and doesn't use a slide that says green. Each run on the screen as Quinn recorded it, with the limit drawn on it in red. The ripple starting 2 milliseconds after lift on every third close after a soak, eight of eight, cause unknown. What a ripple like that is evidence of, and what it isn't. The 40 milliseconds on orbit. Revision C against D, which nobody can explain yet. The blind reads, including the one that missed. Then the two options side by side, what each costs in days and crew time, what each leaves unknown, and the date after which one of them stops being possible. A member asks what the program recommends. A final integrated test of the valve on orbit before anybody accepts anything, ma'am, with the criteria written first. And keep the spacewalk alive until then. In the second row Wendell nods, once, the way he used to at the console.

Exactly right. Status has to show the work as it is: measurements against limits, the trend, the unknowns, and the options with their consequences. Accurate status is what lets governance decide. Integrity in reporting means the people deciding see the same valve you do.

12:10 PM. Lunch recess. Wendell had gone at the start of it, an hour short of the doctor's five, with Arlo driving him home to Byers. The hall smelled like the sandwiches the clerk had ordered, and Hana came out of the witness room with her face set the way it had been on the stand deck in February.

Tallgrass's counsel had found her at the coffee urn at noon. The afternoon was Tallgrass's request, and Hana was Tallgrass's propulsion lead and its witness. Counsel's advice, Hana said, had been friendly and very clear. Stick to the engineering. The board didn't need history. Attachment B had it covered.
Attachment B was on Sam's phone. THE 2059 DISPOSITION OF AR 2207 FOLLOWED THE PROPULSION LEAD'S RECOMMENDATION OF SEPTEMBER 18, 2059.
Garrett's own account had been in the clerk's inbox since 8:50, with the phone call on page one and the time beside it. Attachment B left that out, and his counsel had written it on Monday.

Garrett was at the window at the end of the hall, on his phone, with his back to them. Hana looked at him, and then at Sam. I'm going to say what happened. All of it. I'm telling you first so you know I'm not asking.
Hana says she'll tell the board everything that happened. What should Sam do?
A. Sit Hana and Garrett down together before two, and settle what happens to attachment B.
B. Take Hana off the witness list to spare her, and answer the propulsion questions himself.
C. Tell the chair privately at the recess that Tallgrass has coached its own witness.
D. Tell Hana to keep to the engineering this afternoon, as counsel advised, and leave the history.

It takes eleven minutes in the room with the tissues: Garrett, Hana, counsel, Sam. Sam says the ground rule out loud so it's been said. Nobody in this building tells a witness what to leave out, and nobody's name goes into a submission they haven't read. He asks Hana what she needs. She says to say it in her own words. He asks Garrett whether attachment B is true. Garrett reads it again, slowly, and tells counsel to withdraw it. A one line correction goes to the clerk at 1:48: ATTACHMENT B IS WITHDRAWN. SEE THE CLOSURE HISTORY. At 2:10 Hana tells the board about her kitchen table and the email at 11:52 PM, and about the phone call at 9:40 that came before it, which she's never said out loud. Nobody tells her to stop.

That's a go. Go to the source of the conflict with both people, state the ground rule plainly, and agree a resolution they can both live with: no coaching a witness to leave out facts, and no retaliation for telling them (Code 2.3.5, 5.3.1). It holds because Garrett made it himself.

2:00 PM. Tallgrass's request. Garrett read his account into the record first, standing, from the two pages he'd written at 8:50. He read the dinner and the call at 9:40 and the four minutes and the stand he'd booked over Wendell's slot. Then he said, Nobody did it alone. I did more of it than anybody, and sat down, and at the end of Tallgrass's table Hana put her pen down very carefully.

Then the chair turned the statement of nonconcurrence over and asked why the program manager of record wouldn't sign his own program's waiver. In 2041 I signed off a jet with a doubt behind it, ma'am. The pilot didn't come home. I'm not going to sign another one. He didn't say anything else, and the chair didn't ask him to. On the bench Ruth wrote something with the green pen and didn't look up.

At 2:50 Commander Haddad spoke for the crew, from a sheet all four of them had marked up, two of them in Houston. The crew would fly the workaround if the board accepted the risk in writing, with the data in front of it and the crew's consent asked for and given. The crew wouldn't fly on a waiver that called the ground runs nominal. We'd like to be asked, she said. Not told afterward.

Hale spoke at three, from a page of her own, about sixteen million dollars and eleven governments, and said she'd rather lose the money in public than have the board decide on the calendar. It was the best speech of the day, and she knew it.

At 3:40 the chair closed the testimony. One more thing before the board deliberates. If this request isn't granted, the program and the contractor have nine weeks and a valve. Tell us who you propose should decide what between now and the burn, and what happens when somebody disagrees.

Garrett answered first. Tallgrass built the stage and knew it best, he said, so the prime contractor should hold acceptance authority for the workaround within written limits, and report to the board. Hale's office had put a different note on the program's table: residual risk sits with the sponsor, who owns the objectives. In the fourth row Lorna Whitcombe had written on her pad in capitals and turned it so Sam could see. WHOEVER IT IS, WRITE IT DOWN BEFORE THE WINDOW OPENS.
The chair asks who should decide what between now and the burn. What should Sam propose?
A. Propose that Tallgrass hold acceptance authority for the workaround within written limits.
B. Propose that Hale, as sponsor, accept the residual risk, and report each acceptance to the partners.
C. Propose that the program manager accept risk within limits the board sets, and report each call to the board.
D. Propose a table naming who decides each call, and leave crew risk to the board, with crew consent.

He puts it on the screen with Quinn, because they'd drafted it on Wednesday night, in case. Each decision between now and departure has its own row: who recommends, who decides, who has to agree, who's told. Residual risk to the crew is accepted only by the board, in writing, under its Rule 11, after the crew has given its consent in writing. The program recommends from the data. The contractor can't accept risk on the crew's behalf, and neither can the program manager. The criteria for any final test are written and published before it runs, and nobody changes them after. Anybody on the program can file a dissent; it's written up with the agreed facts and both positions, goes at least two levels up, and costs its author nothing. The chair asks the clerk for a copy. Garrett reads it twice. In the fourth row Lorna turns her pad face down.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Governance means decision rights written down before they're needed: who recommends, who decides, who must consent, with thresholds set in advance and a path for documented dissent. Risk to people is accepted by the authority that matches it, with the people exposed consenting.

Friday, December 15. 7:00 AM. The board's notice had posted at 6:30. ITEM 1: DELIBERATION CONTINUES. DECISION TO BE POSTED BY NOON TUESDAY, DECEMBER 19. Three days ahead of Coquina's manifest. Somebody on the bench had done the arithmetic.

Greaves had run Ruth's statement in full at nine the night before, all eleven minutes of it, without music, under the title I SIGNED IT. By midnight it had been watched more times than anything the feed had run since the AR 2207 record in October. Frances Odum had texted at 12:15. We watched it together. All of us.

On Thursday at 4:20, after the chair adjourned, he'd caught Ruth at the elevator with her coat on. He'd told her it was personal and not about the item, and she'd waited. You heard the short version this afternoon. His name was Leo Marchetti. He was a friend of mine. The mishap board named a different cause, and I'll never know if it was me. Ruth had looked at him for a long moment. No, she'd said. You won't. Thank you for telling me his name. The elevator had come, and she'd gotten on, and that was all.

At 7:40 Frances called. Families of Ares had two hundred and six families on its list, and since nine last night they'd shared two rumors: that the board had grounded Halcyon, and that it was going to fly the crew on a broken valve and say nothing. The families' call was at six that evening. She wanted to know what she could tell them.
They trust you. Most of them. I'd like to keep it that way, so tell me the truth and I'll tell it to them.

Hale's office had sent a line for the families an hour earlier, approved, in bold. The ARA remains committed to a February launch. Tallgrass's communications office had sent one too. It used the word confident twice.
Frances wants to know what she can tell the families this evening. What should Sam do?
A. Wait for Tuesday's ruling, and brief the families on the same day it posts, in person.
B. Forward Hale's line and Tallgrass's statement to Frances, and ask her to send both out.
C. Join Frances's call at six and tell the families where the board stands and when it decides.
D. Tell the families the program expects approval and the launch is on for February.

He's on the families' call at six, from the kitchen in Aurora, with Frances introducing him. He tells them what the board heard, and both options, and what nobody knows yet. He tells them the board decides by noon Tuesday, and that they'll hear it from him the same day, as soon as it posts. He tells them the plan is still a February 18 departure, that a plan isn't a promise, and that the woman who taught him the difference read her life into the record yesterday. A father in Pueblo asks whether the crew will fly on a valve nobody understands. Not without the board accepting the risk in writing, sir, and not without the crew saying yes. I'll tell you which on Tuesday. Frances texts at 6:52. Thank you. That's what I'll say too.

Exactly right. Manage stakeholder expectations with the truth as it stands: what's known, what isn't, when the decision comes, and when they'll hear it. Uncertainty told plainly holds trust better than reassurance that might not hold.
Decision ten. On track for what.

1:30 PM. Watkins, the program room. Tallgrass's communications office had sent a draft statement at noon, for release at five, with a headline in bold. HALCYON ON TRACK FOR FEBRUARY 18 AFTER READINESS REVIEW. Under it was a quote from Garrett about engineering excellence and a space left for a quote from the program manager.
Hale's office had sent its own draft, which agreed with Tallgrass's on the date and on nothing else. Greaves had sent a question at 12:40, one line. Is February 18 a date or a promise?

Quinn had both drafts up on the big screen beside the countdown board, which said 65. Across the road, in flight control, the controllers' poster still said LAUNCH FEB 18 in the biggest letters on it.

Rafa came in with a sandwich and read the headline over Quinn's shoulder. On track for what? The board hasn't decided anything. Quinn said that was the trouble. Everybody had a picture of what the ship was for, and every picture stopped at a date. Rafa's sprint goal stopped at cutoff. The press stopped at liftoff. Since last night the families stopped at the word waiver.
The program charter said what the ship was for in its first line. Nobody had quoted the first line in public in a year.
The headline says on track, and Rafa asks on track for what. What should Sam do about the headline?
A. Tell Tallgrass and Hale's office he won't be quoted until Tuesday, and let them agree a line.
B. Approve Tallgrass's headline as written, and add a line of his own that safety comes first.
C. Sit down with Hale's office and Tallgrass to rework the release around what the ship is for.
D. Write a line that commits the program to a February 18 launch for the families and the public.

It takes until 4:30 and four phone calls, two of them with Hale. What comes out is short, and it's the same words for Greaves, the families, and the high bay. Halcyon exists to get air to Ares Station before its reserve runs out. The readiness board heard two options for a valve that isn't fully understood, and decides by Tuesday. The plan is still a February 18 departure in a window that runs to March 4, the board's decision may change the plan, and if it does the program will say so the same day. Garrett's quote stays, minus the word excellence. Sam's is one sentence. We're going because they need air, and February 18 is the plan for getting it there. Greaves runs it at five without changing a word, and at 5:20, on air, he answers his own question: a plan.

That's a go. Keep the shared vision current and find the root cause of the misunderstanding: each group's picture of success stopped at a date. Restate the vision with the stakeholders, in one set of words for everyone, with the open decision stated honestly.
Decision eleven. Here you close things.

4:30 PM. The light was going orange across the prairie, and from Sam's office window he could see the stand road two miles out, and a truck on it coming in from the blockhouse with its window down an inch.

Wendell's contract had ended at four, and he'd meant to leave on the hour, to beat traffic on I-70 that there wouldn't be. He'd left the console to Arlo without a ceremony, which was the only kind he'd agreed to. Page twelve went with him, in the shirt pocket. Arlo had the stand console now.
Garrett came in without knocking, sat in the chair Peg usually took, and looked out at the same truck.
Well. I said it. In public. My investors watched it at lunch, and two of them called, and one of them said good.

Monday at 7:30 was the all hands, in the high bay, on the pallet jack, nine hundred people. Garrett had a draft on his phone. It said the hearing had shown the strength of Tallgrass's engineering and its commitment to safety, and that it was time to put 2059 behind them and get the ship to the pad.

The stand crew had a version of their own, which Corinne had heard in the break room and written on her legal pad without comment, and she'd left the pad on Sam's desk. Here you close things the month before a review, and the person who says no finds out from the work order.
What do I tell them, Sam? Really.
Garrett asks what he should really tell nine hundred people on Monday. What's Sam's best answer?
A. Suggest a Monday memo from Garrett announcing a new anomaly closure procedure, in force at once.
B. Have security find who leaked the closure record to Greaves, and deal with it firmly.
C. Spend the weekend hearing from the stand crew how closing things really works, then let Garrett speak.
D. Tell Garrett to give the speech as drafted, and reassure the floor that the company is sound.

They spend the weekend listening. On Saturday morning Corinne gets the stand crew in the blockhouse, with coffee and Sam and no Garrett, and asks one question: when something here doesn't look right, what happens next? It takes two hours. On Sunday Garrett sits in the propulsion bay with Hana's team for three. On Monday at 7:30 he stands on the pallet jack and doesn't use the draft. He tells nine hundred people about a phone call at 9:40 at night in September 2059, and says the company he built made a call like that feel normal, and that he's the one who made it. Then he reads three changes the stand crew wrote. No anomaly closes in the month before a review without independent sign off. Every closure carries a concurrence from someone outside the team. Anybody can stop a closure by filing a dissent, which goes two levels up, with their name protected if they ask. At the back by the doors Arlo writes the third one on his glove.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Support organizational change by assessing the culture first, with the people who live in it: what gets rewarded, how decisions are really made. Leaders model the change by owning their part, and the new rules come from the people they're meant to protect.
Monday, December 18. 5:40 AM. The kitchen in Aurora, with the coffee maker going. One way fourteen minutes and forty seconds.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 4206. One way, 14 minutes 40 seconds. Margin, 253 days. Hi, Dad. Log fifty five. Sol 4206. We watched the hearing. Most of the station, in the galley, on the big screen, fifteen minutes behind you. Okonkwo brought the good chairs over from the plant office. Malik kept score of the coffee on the bench, which he says looked bad even from here. And then Ruth Calder. I'd never seen her. I've read about the Petrel since I was nine, because you went quiet whenever it came on, and I thought that was what grownups did about it. She said I signed it. I counted three times. Nobody in the galley said anything for a long time afterward, and then Pilar went and made tea for everybody, which is what Pilar does. And then you. One sentence. A jet, and a doubt, and a pilot who didn't come home. Two hundred people turned around in their chairs to look at me, Dad. I didn't know what my face was doing. So I'm going to ask you something I've never asked. Why did you leave the Air Force? I was five. I asked Mom once, when I was eleven, and she said it was yours to tell, and that someday you would. I remember Arizona a little. A hangar that smelled like hot rubber. A man who let me sit in the jet and called me Captain and put his hat on my head, and the hat had a patch on it with a little black bag, like a doctor's. I've always thought that part was a dream. Was it him? The sleeve's been off a week. The pink is going white at the edges. Mom's watch says it's five in the morning there, so you're up. Mine's 253. Okonkwo's is 260, which is the board's. Arrival's day 262. Minus nine, minus two. The other place is coming along. It's still not in my number. Soon. Take your time with it. I mean that. But answer it. Log fifty five. Ada out.
He watched it twice. The second time he stopped it on her hands, which were flat on the table in front of her, the way Quinn's went when the news was bad.

The photograph was in a drawer in Ada's room, under her old swim team ribbons, where Grace had put it in 2042 and where he'd known it was every day since. A hangar in Arizona in April light. Ada at four, on an upturned helmet bag. Beside her a man in a flight suit, crouched down with his cap on her head, laughing at something off the edge of the frame. The patch on the cap had a black doctor's bag on it, and the word DOC.

At 6:10 he called Tucson. Ray picked up on the second ring, the way he had for twenty one years. Saw you on the feed. Ada wants to know why I left. A screen door, and the sound of Ray sitting down on something that creaked. Then tell her. She's grown. She's on Mars. She can carry a story. And after a while: Tell her you don't know, too. That's the part you never say. The jet doesn't care how you feel. Doesn't mean you don't get to feel it.

The board would post its decision by noon tomorrow. At 7:30 that night he sat down at the kitchen table, in his own chair, with the photograph propped against the fruit bowl and the coffee maker off, and pressed record.
Ada asks why Sam left the Air Force. What should he tell her tonight?
A. Tell her about Leo and the jet, and leave out that he'll never know if it was him.
B. Record the whole story tonight, and send it after the crew launches and the worst month is past.
C. Keep tonight's log light, tell her the hearing went fine, and save Arizona for another night.
D. Tell her the whole story tonight, including the part he'll never know.

The first try he stops at the hangar. The second he stops at the form. The third he lets run, forty minutes, and sends. He tells her about a surge week in April 2041, and a Thursday, and a jet with a hydraulic pressure indication that came and went, and the hour he'd have taken to chase it if there'd been an hour. He tells her about the man in the photograph, Captain Leo Marchetti, call sign Doc, who walked out to the jet at one in the afternoon. Then he says it the way it happened. He asked me, 'Is she good, Chief?' Ordinary voice, like every other day. I said, 'She's good, sir.' I'd have said it the same way that morning. I don't know if it was true, Ada. I never will. He tells her the mishap board named a different cause, and that he's never believed that was all of it, and that the not knowing is what he's been carrying since. He tells her that's why he left, and why for twenty years his signature only ever meant a building. Then he tells her the board decides by noon tomorrow, between two options, and that the ship isn't on track for anything yet. It's waiting on a valve. He doesn't do the voice. There isn't one for this.

Exactly right. She asked you a straight question, and she's owed a straight answer, about the ship and about you, including the part you don't know. The voice was always a half truth. She asked for the whole one.

Monday, December 18. 9:02 PM. He sent it, and turned the tablet face down, and sat at the table with the photograph until the coffee maker's clock said ten. Grace's red glass pepper ornament hung on the knob of the cabinet over the coffee maker, where he'd hung it last Christmas too, because he didn't know what else to do with it.

Tuesday, December 19. 11:58 AM. The program room at Watkins, with everybody who could fit in it and some who couldn't. Quinn had the board's page on the big screen two minutes before it posted, refreshing, and when it came nobody said anything until they'd all read it twice.

INDEPENDENT READINESS BOARD DECISION ITEM 1 SESSION OF DECEMBER 14, 2062 POSTED DECEMBER 19, 2062, 11:58 AM. ITEM 1. REQUEST FOR WAIVER 62-14: NOT APPROVED. THE STATEMENT OF NONCONCURRENCE OF THE PROGRAM MANAGER OF RECORD IS PART OF THE RECORD.. CR 62-311: THE BOARD DEFERS THE CHOICE BETWEEN THE WORKAROUND AND REPLACEMENT BY SPACEWALK. A FINAL INTEGRATED TEST OF MOIV-1 WILL BE RUN ON ORBIT ON TUESDAY, JANUARY 30, 2063, THE DAY THE WINDOW OPENS. PASS CRITERIA WILL BE SET BY THE BOARD WITH THE PROGRAM, THE CREW, AND FLIGHT OPERATIONS, AND PUBLISHED BEFORE THE TEST.. THE REPLACEMENT VALVE WILL BE COMPLETED AND FLOWN WITH THE CREW ON JANUARY 9, SO THAT REPLACEMENT REMAINS POSSIBLE.. RESIDUAL RISK TO THE CREW ON THIS ITEM MAY BE ACCEPTED ONLY BY THIS BOARD, IN WRITING, WITH THE WRITTEN CONSENT OF THE CREW. NO OTHER PARTY MAY ACCEPT IT.. THE BOARD ADOPTS THE PROGRAM'S DECISION TABLE AS ATTACHMENT 1.. AR 2207 CLOSURE HISTORY: ACCOUNT OF G. LYLE ENTERED.. DISCLOSURES OF MEMBER CALDER AND OF THE PROGRAM MANAGER MINUTED.. VOTE: 6 TO 0 ON THE WAIVER. MEMBER FERRIS VOTED AGAINST THE WAIVER AS WRITTEN. 5 TO 1 ON THE DEFERRAL. MEMBER FERRIS DISSENTS IN PART AND WOULD APPROVE THE WORKAROUND NOW UNDER WRITTEN RISK ACCEPTANCE. DISSENT ATTACHED.. MEMBER CALDER CONCURS AND ADDS: THE CRITERIA MUST BE PUBLISHED BEFORE THE TEST.. E. QUAYLE, CHAIR

Not approved. He read it, and then he read the dissent, which was two careful pages from a man who'd have flown the workaround today and said exactly why. It was a better argument than Garrett's had been. It was in the record, where somebody in January could find it.

At 12:04 he called Haddad, and she'd already read it, because the crew got the board's postings now, the same minute as everybody else. January 30, she said. We'll be up there for it. Good. I'd rather be in the room.

At 12:10 Hale's office forwarded a line from the partners' finance committee. It had met on Monday and held the sixteen million over until the board ruled, and it would take the money up again at its first meeting in January.

At 12:30 he was on the line with the families, as he'd told them he'd be on Friday, and he read them the decision and said what it meant and what it didn't. Frances read the dissent out loud to them herself, all of it, because she said they should hear the other side from somebody who wasn't selling it.

At Watkins, on the stand crew's whiteboard in the blockhouse, somebody had copied the decision's last line in marker under the three rules from Monday. NO OTHER PARTY MAY ACCEPT IT. Arlo had underlined OTHER.
Wednesday, December 20. 5:40 AM. One way fourteen minutes and thirty one seconds.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 4208. One way, 14 minutes 31 seconds. Margin, 251 days. Hi, Dad. Log fifty six. Sol 4208. I didn't wait six sols. I watched yours three times and then I went and sat in Bay C with the tomatoes for a while, which is where I go. Leo. I've got a name for the hat now. I'm going to say it in the galley tonight, if that's all right with you, because Malik asked who you were talking about and I want to tell it right. You said you'll never know. I believe you. I live on a station where nobody knows half of what we'd like to, and we get up anyway. I'd like you to stop carrying it by yourself, Dad. It's heavy, and you're old. And thank you for the ship. Waiting on a valve is a real answer. I can plan around a real answer. 251. Okonkwo's 258. Arrival day 260. Same minus nine. Love you. Log fifty six. Ada out.

He watched it twice. Then he got up and took the photograph to the refrigerator and put it there, under page one and the magnet shaped like Colorado, with Leo laughing at whatever was off the edge of it, and left it there.

At 10:40 the mail came. A long white envelope, green ink, Golden postmark, posted the afternoon the board's decision went up and not one hour before. Page thirteen. He read it standing at the counter, beside his own envelope, still unsealed under his keys, with the photocopy in it and STILL ASKING beside the third row. He read the ten forty five line four times. SIGNED LINE 1. LET LINE 2 GO. There was nothing else on the page but what she'd written in 2036. She'd kept her side of it exactly.
He'd done most of this week the slow way, in writing, through the door everybody had agreed to use. It hadn't felt like winning anything. Ruth would have said that was how you could tell.

Over the high bay doors, twenty miles east, the clock said 60. Under it, on the program room's whiteboard, Quinn had written a second date in marker for the first time, and drawn a box around it. TEST TUE JAN 30.
